items.stem: Which list contains only SI base quantities?
items.answer: mass, length, time, temperature
items.markingKey: The SI base quantities are mass, length, time, current, temperature and amount of substance.

items.stem: Explain why an equation that is homogeneous may still be physically incorrect.
items.answer: Homogeneity only checks the units; the equation may have a missing or wrong pure number (such as ½ or 2π), or a missing dimensionless term, which units cannot reveal.
items.markingKey: units the same does not check numerical constants [1]; example such as ½ or 2π or missing term [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that the equation s = ut + ½at² is homogeneous.
items.answer: s: m; ut: (m s⁻¹)(s) = m; ½at²: (m s⁻²)(s²) = m. Every term has units of m, so it is homogeneous (½ has no unit).
items.markingKey: units of ut = m [1]; units of at² = m and conclusion [1] [2]

items.stem: A textbook states that the resistance R of a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A is R = ρL/A. Determine the SI base units of ρ. Show your working.
items.answer: kg m³ s⁻³ A⁻²
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement ρ = RA/L = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻² × m² ÷ m [1]; kg m³ s⁻³ A⁻² [1] [3]

items.stem: In an engineering model, the rate of thermal energy flow Q/t through a slab of area A and thickness x with temperature difference ΔT is Q/t = kAΔT/x. Determine the SI base units of k. Show your working.
items.answer: kg m s⁻³ K⁻¹
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement k = (Q/t)x/(AΔT) = kg m² s⁻³ × m ÷ (m² K) [1]; kg m s⁻³ K⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: During a project, Aisha finds that the energy E of a photon of frequency f is E = hf. (a) Explain why the equation must be homogeneous if it is correct. (b) State the SI base units of force and of energy.
items.answer: (a) Quantities can only be equated or added if they are the same kind of quantity, so every term must have the same base units. (b) force kg m s⁻²; energy kg m² s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) only like quantities can be equal/added [1]; same base units each term [1] [2] (b) force [1]; energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Which unit is an SI base unit?
items.answer: ampere
items.markingKey: The ampere (current) is a base unit; coulomb, volt and newton are derived.

items.stem: Show that the equation v² = u² + 2as is homogeneous.
items.answer: v² and u²: m² s⁻²; as: (m s⁻²)(m) = m² s⁻². All terms have the same base units.
items.markingKey: v², u² in m² s⁻² [1]; 2as in m² s⁻² and conclusion [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a base quantity and a derived quantity, giving one example of each.
items.answer: A base quantity is one of the six chosen independent quantities (e.g. mass, unit kg); a derived quantity is defined in terms of base quantities (e.g. speed = distance/time, unit m s⁻¹).
items.markingKey: base: fundamental/independent with example [1]; derived: defined from base quantities with example [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the kilogram and the second are called base units but the newton is not.
items.answer: The kilogram and second are defined independently; the newton is defined from them through F = ma (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²), so it is a derived unit.
items.markingKey: kg and s defined independently [1]; N derived from F = ma as kg m s⁻² [1] [2]

items.stem: A textbook states that the frequency f of oscillation of a mass m on a spring of stiffness k is f = C√(k/m). Determine the SI base units of C. Show your working.
items.answer: no units (it is dimensionless)
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement k/m = kg s⁻² ÷ kg = s⁻², √ gives s⁻¹, same as f [1]; no units (it is dimensionless) [1] [3]

items.stem: A student reads that the energy E of a photon of frequency f is E = hf. Determine the SI base units of h. Show your working.
items.answer: kg m² s⁻¹
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement h = E/f = kg m² s⁻² ÷ s⁻¹ [1]; kg m² s⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: A data booklet states that the gravitational force between masses M and m a distance r apart is F = GMm/r². (a) State the difference between a base unit and a derived unit. (b) Explain why the equation must be homogeneous if it is correct.
items.answer: (a) Base units are the defined SI units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol); derived units are combinations of base units. (b) Quantities can only be equated or added if they are the same kind of quantity, so every term must have the same base units.
items.markingKey: (a) base units listed/independent [1]; derived from combinations [1] [2] (b) only like quantities can be equal/added [1]; same base units each term [1] [2]

items.stem: A data booklet states that the energy E of a photon of frequency f is E = hf. (a) Determine the SI base units of h. (b) Suggest why a homogeneous equation may still be wrong. (c) State the SI base units of force and of energy.
items.answer: (a) kg m² s⁻¹ (b) It may have the wrong dimensionless constant or a missing dimensionless term. (c) force kg m s⁻²; energy kg m² s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) h = E/f = kg m² s⁻² ÷ s⁻¹ [1]; = kg m² s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) It may have the wrong dimensionless constant or a missing dimensionless term [1] (c) force [1]; energy [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the value of the prefix pico (p)?
items.answer: 10⁻¹²
items.markingKey: pico = 10⁻¹².

items.stem: Explain why a physicist would write 0.000 000 52 m as 520 nm or 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ m.
items.answer: Prefixes and standard form make very small or large numbers easier to read and compare, reduce copying errors and show the number of significant figures clearly.
items.markingKey: easier to read/compare [1]; shows significant figures / fewer errors [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the conversion from cm² to m² involves dividing by 10⁴ and not by 100.
items.answer: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = (100 cm)² = 10⁴ cm²; the prefix factor is squared because area has two length dimensions.
items.markingKey: (100)² [1]; prefix squared for area [1] [2]

items.stem: Express a wire diameter of 1.14 mm in m, in standard form.
The cross-sectional area of a component is quoted as 120 cm². Convert this to m², explaining your conversion factor.
items.markingKey: 1 cm = 10⁻² m [1]; factor raised to power 2 = 10⁻⁴ [1]; 1.2 × 10⁻² m² [1] [3]

items.stem: Mei is writing a report on an optical experiment using light of wavelength 450 nm and a wire of diameter 0.32 mm. (a) Express the wavelength in metres in standard form. (b) Calculate the frequency of the light (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). (c) State the frequency using a suitable prefix.
items.markingKey: (a) nm = 10⁻⁹: 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m [1] (b) f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.67 × 10¹⁴ Hz [1] [2] (c) THz = 10¹² Hz: 667 THz [1]

items.stem: What is the value of the prefix tera (T)?
items.answer: 10¹²
items.markingKey: tera = 10¹².

items.stem: Estimate the kinetic energy of a car travelling on a motorway, stating the values you use.
items.markingKey: sensible m and v [1]; E ≈ 10⁵–10⁶ J [1] [2]

items.stem: Estimate the pressure exerted on the floor by a person standing on both feet, stating your estimates.
items.answer: Weight ≈ 700 N; area of two feet ≈ 2 × 0.025 m² = 0.05 m²; p ≈ 700/0.05 ≈ 1.4 × 10⁴ Pa.
items.markingKey: sensible weight and area [1]; p ≈ 10⁴ Pa [1] [2]

items.stem: Estimate the energy needed to climb a flight of stairs in a house, stating your estimates.
items.markingKey: sensible m and h [1]; E ≈ 2 kJ [1] [2]

items.stem: Estimate the pressure on the ground under an elephant standing on four feet. State the values you use.
items.answer: about 1 × 10⁵ Pa (using m ≈ 5000 kg, area of each foot ≈ 0.1 m²)
items.markingKey: sensible estimates (m ≈ 5000 kg, area of each foot ≈ 0.1 m²) [1]; p = F/A applied [1]; answer within an order of magnitude of 1 × 10⁵ Pa [1] [3]

items.stem: Estimate the power of a student running up a 3 m flight of stairs in 3 s. State the values you use.
items.answer: about 600 W (using m ≈ 60 kg, h ≈ 3 m, t ≈ 3 s)
items.markingKey: sensible estimates (m ≈ 60 kg, h ≈ 3 m, t ≈ 3 s) [1]; P = mgh/t applied [1]; answer within an order of magnitude of 600 W [1] [3]

items.stem: Chloe is writing a report on an optical experiment using light of wavelength 589 nm and a wire of diameter 0.32 mm. (a) Express the wavelength in metres in standard form. (b) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire in m². (c) State the frequency using a suitable prefix.
items.markingKey: (a) nm = 10⁻⁹: 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m [1] (b) A = πd²/4 with d = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m² [1] [2] (c) THz = 10¹² Hz: 509 THz [1]

items.stem: Arjun is writing a report on an optical experiment using light of wavelength 520 nm and a wire of diameter 0.32 mm. (a) Express the wavelength in metres in standard form. (b) Calculate the frequency of the light (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). (c) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire in m².
items.markingKey: (a) nm = 10⁻⁹: 5.20 × 10⁻⁷ m [1] (b) f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 5.20 × 10⁻⁷ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.77 × 10¹⁴ Hz [1] [2] (c) A = πd²/4 with d = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m² [1] [2]

items.stem: Which describes a systematic error?
options: An error caused only by a mistake in arithmetic
An error that makes readings scatter randomly about the true value
An error that is removed by averaging many readings
An error that makes every reading too large (or too small) by the same amount or proportion
items.answer: An error that makes every reading too large (or too small) by the same amount or proportion
items.markingKey: Systematic errors shift all readings in the same direction, e.g. a zero error; repeating does not remove them.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a systematic error and a random error, giving an example of each.
items.answer: A systematic error shifts all readings the same way (e.g. a zero error on a meter); a random error causes readings to scatter unpredictably about the mean (e.g. reaction time when using a stopwatch).
items.markingKey: systematic: same direction/size with example [1]; random: scatter with example [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why taking repeat readings does not reduce a systematic error.
items.answer: Every reading is shifted by the same amount in the same direction, so the mean is shifted too; the error must be found and corrected (e.g. by subtracting a zero error or recalibrating).
items.markingKey: all readings shifted equally / mean also shifted [1]; must correct the instrument or reading [1] [2]

items.stem: The p.d. across a resistor is 3.60 ± 0.05 V and the current is 0.120 ± 0.005 A. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the resistance.
items.markingKey: %R = %V + %I = 1.4 + 4.2 = 5.6%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The p.d. across a resistor is 5.20 ± 0.05 V and the current is 0.320 ± 0.005 A. Calculate the resistance and its absolute uncertainty, giving both to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: R = V/I = 16.25 Ω [1]; %R = 0.96 + 1.6 = 2.5% [1]; ΔR = 0.4 Ω [1]; R quoted to same decimal place as ΔR [1] [4]

items.stem: A metal cylinder has mass 77.0 ± 0.1 g, diameter 2.00 ± 0.01 cm and length 3.20 ± 0.05 cm. Its density is ρ = 4m/(πd²L). Calculate the density in g cm⁻³ and its absolute uncertainty.

In a practical class in Doha, the resistivity of a wire is found from ρ = RA/L, with R = 4.2 ± 0.1 Ω, L = 1.500 ± 0.002 m and d = 0.32 ± 0.01 mm. (a) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire. (b) Explain why the micrometer should be checked for zero error before use.
items.answer: (a) 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m² (b) A zero error is systematic and would shift every diameter reading, giving an inaccurate area and resistivity.
items.markingKey: (a) A = πd²/4 = π × (3.2 × 10⁻⁴)²/4 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m² [1] [2] (b) zero error systematic [1]; shifts all readings/affects ρ via d² [1] [2]

items.stem: In an AS Physics lesson in Singapore, the resistivity of a wire is found from ρ = RA/L, with R = 6.8 ± 0.1 Ω, L = 1.200 ± 0.002 m and d = 0.40 ± 0.01 mm. (a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the resistivity. (b) Explain why the micrometer should be checked for zero error before use.
items.answer: (a) 6.6% (b) A zero error is systematic and would shift every diameter reading, giving an inaccurate area and resistivity.
items.markingKey: (a) %R + 2%d + %L = 1.5 + 5.0 + 0.17 (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 6.6% with unit [1] [3] (b) zero error systematic [1]; shifts all readings/affects ρ via d² [1] [2]

items.stem: A set of readings is close together but all far from the true value. The readings are …
items.answer: precise but not accurate
items.markingKey: Precise: small spread; accurate: close to the true value.

items.stem: Which error can be reduced by taking repeat readings and averaging?
items.answer: Random error
items.markingKey: Averaging reduces random scatter; it does not affect systematic error.

items.stem: A student measures the period of a pendulum by timing 20 oscillations. Explain why this reduces the percentage uncertainty in the period.
items.answer: The absolute uncertainty in the timing (reaction time) is about the same whatever the total time, so dividing by 20 makes the uncertainty in one period 20 times smaller; the percentage uncertainty is reduced.
items.markingKey: uncertainty in total time roughly constant [1]; divided over 20 periods / larger time gives smaller percentage [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a quantity that depends on d² has a percentage uncertainty twice that of d.
items.answer: d² = d × d; for a product the percentage uncertainties add, so % in d² = % in d + % in d = 2 × % in d.
items.markingKey: product rule: percentages add [1]; d × d gives 2 × % [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why an ammeter with a zero error can give precise but inaccurate readings.
items.answer: The readings may be close together (small random scatter, so precise), but each is shifted from the true value by the zero error (so not accurate).
items.markingKey: precise: small scatter [1]; inaccurate: shifted by zero error [1] [2]

items.stem: The diameter of a ball bearing is measured as 18.2 ± 0.1 mm. What is the percentage uncertainty in its volume?
The diameter of a ball bearing is measured as 20.0 ± 0.1 mm. Work out the percentage uncertainty in its volume.
items.markingKey: V ∝ d³, so %V = 3 × 0.50% = 1.5%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A metal cylinder has mass 52.8 ± 0.1 g, diameter 2.20 ± 0.01 cm and length 3.20 ± 0.05 cm. Its density is ρ = 4m/(πd²L). Calculate the percentage uncertainty in ρ.
items.markingKey: %ρ = %m + 2%d + %L = 0.19 + 2 × 0.45 + 1.6 = 2.7%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A trolley passes a mark at 15.6 ± 0.1 cm and a second mark at 77.4 ± 0.1 cm, taking 2.45 ± 0.05 s. Calculate the average speed in m s⁻¹ and its percentage uncertainty.

Grace determines the resistivity of a metal wire using ρ = RA/L. The measurements are L = 1.500 ± 0.002 m, diameter d = 0.28 ± 0.01 mm and R = 5.6 ± 0.1 Ω. (a) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire. (b) Calculate the resistivity.
items.markingKey: (a) A = πd²/4 = π × (2.8 × 10⁻⁴)²/4 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m² [1] [2] (b) ρ = RA/L = 5.6 × 6.16 × 10⁻⁸/1.500 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.30 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia determines the resistivity of a metal wire using ρ = RA/L. The measurements are L = 1.000 ± 0.002 m, diameter d = 0.36 ± 0.01 mm and R = 5.6 ± 0.1 Ω. (a) Calculate the resistivity. (b) Explain why the micrometer should be checked for zero error before use.
items.answer: (a) 5.70 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m (b) A zero error is systematic and would shift every diameter reading, giving an inaccurate area and resistivity.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = RA/L = 5.6 × 1.02 × 10⁻⁷/1.000 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.70 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m [1] [2] (b) zero error systematic [1]; shifts all readings/affects ρ via d² [1] [2]

items.stem: Which list contains only vector quantities?
items.answer: displacement, acceleration, momentum
items.markingKey: All three have direction.

items.stem: Explain why the resultant of two forces of 6 N and 8 N can have any value between 2 N and 14 N.
items.answer: When the forces are in the same direction the resultant is the sum, 14 N; in opposite directions it is the difference, 2 N; at other angles it takes intermediate values.
items.markingKey: same direction gives 14 N [1]; opposite gives 2 N, intermediate otherwise [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why resolving a force into two perpendicular components is useful.
items.answer: Perpendicular components act independently, so the effects in each direction can be analysed separately (e.g. for motion on a slope or projectiles).
items.markingKey: components independent [1]; allows each direction to be treated separately with example [1] [2]

items.stem: A force of 50 N acts at 20° to the vertical on a bracket. Determine the vertical component of the force.
items.markingKey: 50 cos 20° = 47.0 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A force of 40 N acts at 30° to the vertical on a bracket. Calculate the vertical and horizontal components of the force.
items.answer: vertical 34.6 N; horizontal 20.0 N
items.markingKey: 40 cos 30° = 34.6 N [1]; 40 sin 30° = 20.0 N [1]; correct assignment [1] [3]

items.stem: A crate of weight 240 N is held at rest on a smooth slope of angle 20° by a rope parallel to the slope. (a) State the difference between a scalar and a vector, using weight and mass as examples. (b) Calculate the component of the weight parallel to the slope.
items.answer: (a) Weight is a vector (magnitude and direction, downwards); mass is a scalar (magnitude only). (b) 82.1 N
items.markingKey: (a) definition [1]; weight vector, mass scalar [1] [2] (b) W sin θ = 240 sin 20° (method/substitution) [1]; answer 82.1 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which list contains only vector quantities? (b) A ball moving at 6 m s⁻¹ rebounds from a wall at 4 m s⁻¹ along the same line. What is the magnitude of its change in velocity?
items.answer: (a) displacement, acceleration, momentum (b) 10 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) All three have direction. (b) Taking towards the wall positive: Δv = −4 − 6 = −10 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why a car going around a bend at constant speed has a changing velocity.
items.answer: Velocity is a vector; its direction changes on the bend so the velocity changes although its magnitude (speed) is constant.
items.markingKey: velocity has direction [1]; direction changes [1] [2]

items.stem: A child pulls a suitcase with a force of 250 N along its handle, which is at 20° to the horizontal. What is the horizontal component of the force?
Two forces of 12 N and 4.0 N act at right angles on a small ring. Work out the magnitude of the resultant force.
items.markingKey: √(12² + 4.0²) = 12.6 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tennis ball hits a wall at 6.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 9.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the change in velocity, stating its direction.
items.answer: 15 m s⁻¹ away from the wall (opposite to the initial velocity)
items.markingKey: sign convention: Δv = (−9.0) − 6.0 [1]; magnitude 15 m s⁻¹ [1]; direction away from the wall [1] [3]

items.stem: Aisha walks 12 km due east and then 2.5 km due north. Calculate the magnitude of the displacement and its direction.
items.answer: 12.3 km, 11.8° north of east
items.markingKey: Pythagoras: √(12² + 2.5²) [1] = 12.3 km [1]; trigonometry for angle: 11.8° north of east [1] [3]

items.stem: A box of weight 300 N rests on a ramp inclined at 35° to the horizontal in a warehouse in Lagos. (a) State the difference between a scalar and a vector, using weight and mass as examples. (b) Calculate the component of the weight perpendicular to the slope. (c) The angle of the slope is increased. Explain how the two components change.
items.answer: (a) Weight is a vector (magnitude and direction, downwards); mass is a scalar (magnitude only). (b) 246 N (c) The parallel component (W sin θ) increases and the perpendicular component (W cos θ) decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) definition [1]; weight vector, mass scalar [1] [2] (b) W cos θ = 300 cos 35° (method/substitution) [1]; answer 246 N with unit [1] [2] (c) parallel increases [1]; perpendicular decreases [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the newton expressed in SI base units?
items.answer: kg m s⁻²
items.markingKey: F = ma, so N = kg × m s⁻² = kg m s⁻².

items.stem: A student claims that kinetic energy could be given by E = mv. Use base units to show that this is impossible.
items.answer: mv has base units kg m s⁻¹, but energy has base units kg m² s⁻², so the equation is not homogeneous.
items.markingKey: units of mv = kg m s⁻¹ [1]; energy kg m² s⁻², not equal so wrong [1] [2]

items.stem: In an engineering model, the speed v of a wave on a string of tension T and mass per unit length μ is v = √(T/μ). Determine the SI base units of μ. Show your working.
items.answer: kg m⁻¹
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement μ = T/v² = kg m s⁻² ÷ m² s⁻² [1]; kg m⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: A textbook states that the gravitational force between masses M and m a distance r apart is F = GMm/r². Determine the SI base units of G. Show your working.
items.answer: kg⁻¹ m³ s⁻²
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement G = Fr²/(Mm) = kg m s⁻² × m² ÷ kg² [1]; kg⁻¹ m³ s⁻² [1] [3]

items.stem: During a project, Noah finds that the frequency f of oscillation of a mass m on a spring of stiffness k is f = C√(k/m). (a) State the difference between a base unit and a derived unit. (b) Suggest why a homogeneous equation may still be wrong. (c) State the SI base units of force and of energy.
items.answer: (a) Base units are the defined SI units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol); derived units are combinations of base units. (b) It may have the wrong dimensionless constant or a missing dimensionless term. (c) force kg m s⁻²; energy kg m² s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) base units listed/independent [1]; derived from combinations [1] [2] (b) It may have the wrong dimensionless constant or a missing dimensionless term [1] (c) force [1]; energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the best estimate of the mass of an adult person?
items.answer: 70 kg
items.markingKey: A typical adult has a mass of about 60–80 kg.

items.stem: Explain why 1 mm³ is equal to 10⁻⁹ m³.
items.answer: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so 1 mm³ = (10⁻³ m)³ = 10⁻⁹ m³.
items.markingKey: prefix value 10⁻³ [1]; cubed for volume [1] [2]

items.stem: Express a capacitor of 7.05 µF in F, in standard form.
The cross-sectional area of a component is quoted as 7.9 mm². Convert this to m², explaining your conversion factor.
items.markingKey: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m [1]; factor raised to power 2 = 10⁻⁶ [1]; 7.9 × 10⁻⁶ m² [1] [3]

items.stem: A laser in a practical class in Nairobi emits light of wavelength 450 nm. It is used to measure a wire of diameter 0.32 mm. (a) Express the wavelength in metres in standard form. (b) Calculate the frequency of the light (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). (c) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire in m². (d) State the frequency using a suitable prefix.
items.markingKey: (a) nm = 10⁻⁹: 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m [1] (b) f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.67 × 10¹⁴ Hz [1] [2] (c) A = πd²/4 with d = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m² [1] [2] (d) THz = 10¹² Hz: 667 THz [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A set of readings is close together but all far from the true value. The readings are … (b) State what is meant by the precision of a measurement.
items.answer: (a) precise but not accurate (b) How close repeated readings are to each other (small spread / scatter).
items.markingKey: (a) Precise: small spread; accurate: close to the true value. (b) closeness of repeated readings to each other [1]

items.stem: A digital stopwatch reads to 0.01 s. Explain why the uncertainty in a hand-timed interval is larger than 0.01 s.
items.answer: Human reaction time at starting and stopping (about 0.1–0.2 s) is much larger than the resolution of the watch, so it dominates the uncertainty.
items.markingKey: reaction time [1]; much larger than 0.01 s resolution [1] [2]

items.stem: Four measurements of the acceleration of free fall are 2.71, 2.71, 2.72, 2.69 (same unit). The accepted value is 2.7. Describe the readings in terms of accuracy and precision, and suggest what type of error is most likely present.
items.answer: They are precise and accurate. Mainly random error; no systematic shift is evident.
items.markingKey: precision judged from spread [1]; accuracy judged from mean vs accepted value [1]; correct error type [1] [3]

items.stem: A trolley passes a mark at 22.5 ± 0.1 cm and a second mark at 74.5 ± 0.1 cm, taking 3.10 ± 0.05 s. Calculate the absolute uncertainty in the distance between the marks.
items.markingKey: difference: add absolute uncertainties = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.20 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A metal cylinder has mass 77.0 ± 0.1 g, diameter 2.20 ± 0.01 cm and length 4.50 ± 0.05 cm. Its density is ρ = 4m/(πd²L). Calculate the percentage uncertainty in ρ.
items.markingKey: %ρ = %m + 2%d + %L = 0.13 + 2 × 0.45 + 1.1 = 2.2%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a college physics laboratory in Cairo, the resistivity of a wire is found from ρ = RA/L, with R = 4.2 ± 0.1 Ω, L = 1.200 ± 0.002 m and d = 0.32 ± 0.01 mm. (a) Calculate the resistivity. (b) State which measurement contributes most to the uncertainty and suggest how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) 2.81 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m (b) The diameter (its percentage is doubled); measure with a micrometer at several points along the wire and average.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = RA/L = 4.2 × 8.04 × 10⁻⁸/1.200 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.81 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m [1] [2] (b) diameter identified [1]; micrometer/repeat at different places [1] [2]

items.stem: An aircraft flies north while a wind blows from the west. Explain why its velocity relative to the ground is not due north.
items.answer: The ground velocity is the vector sum of the air velocity (north) and the wind velocity (east), so the resultant points east of north.
items.markingKey: vector addition of air and wind velocity [1]; resultant east of north [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how to find the resultant of two non-perpendicular forces by scale drawing.
items.answer: Choose a scale, draw the first force to scale, draw the second from its tip at the correct angle (tip to tail), then measure the length and angle of the line from start to end.
items.markingKey: scale and tip-to-tail [1]; closing side measured for magnitude [1]; direction measured [1] [3]

items.stem: A rope pulls a sledge with a force of 64 N at 40° above the horizontal. Determine the horizontal component of the force.
items.markingKey: 64 cos 40° = 49.0 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A skier of weight 200 N stands on a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. (a) State the size of the normal contact force from the slope, explaining your answer. (b) The angle of the slope is increased. Explain how the two components change.
items.answer: (a) 173 N, because there is no acceleration perpendicular to the slope. (b) The parallel component (W sin θ) increases and the perpendicular component (W cos θ) decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) equal to the perpendicular component [1]; no perpendicular acceleration [1] [2] (b) parallel increases [1]; perpendicular decreases [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the joule expressed in SI base units?
items.answer: kg m² s⁻²
items.markingKey: W = Fs: (kg m s⁻²)(m) = kg m² s⁻².

items.stem: Show that the equation T = 2π√(l/g) for a pendulum is homogeneous.
items.answer: l/g has units m ÷ m s⁻² = s², so √(l/g) has units s, the same as T; 2π has no units.
items.markingKey: l/g gives s² [1]; square root gives s, same as T [1] [2]

items.stem: A textbook states that the drag force F on a car moving at speed v is F = kv². Determine the SI base units of k. Show your working.
items.answer: kg m⁻¹
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement k = F/v² = kg m s⁻² ÷ m² s⁻² [1]; kg m⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: A physicist proposes that the energy E of a photon of frequency f is E = hf. Determine the SI base units of h. Show your working.
items.answer: kg m² s⁻¹
items.markingKey: base units of each other quantity identified [1]; rearrangement h = E/f = kg m² s⁻² ÷ s⁻¹ [1]; kg m² s⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: During a project, Jonas finds that the pressure p exerted by a fluid of density ρ flowing at speed v against a wall is p = Cρv². (a) Determine the SI base units of C. (b) Suggest why a homogeneous equation may still be wrong. (c) State the SI base units of force and of energy.
items.answer: (a) no units (it is dimensionless) (b) It may have the wrong dimensionless constant or a missing dimensionless term. (c) force kg m s⁻²; energy kg m² s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) ρv² = kg m⁻³ × m² s⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻², same as pressure [1]; = no units (it is dimensionless) [1] [2] (b) It may have the wrong dimensionless constant or a missing dimensionless term [1] (c) force [1]; energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the best estimate of the wavelength of visible light?
items.markingKey: Visible light: 400–700 nm, about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Estimate the energy needed to climb a flight of stairs in a house, stating your estimates. (b) Estimate the kinetic energy of a car travelling on a motorway, stating the values you use.
items.markingKey: (a) sensible m and h [1]; E ≈ 2 kJ [1] [2] (b) sensible m and v [1]; E ≈ 10⁵–10⁶ J [1] [2]

items.stem: Express a current of 50 mA in A, in standard form.
Make a reasoned estimate of the mass of air in a room 5 m × 4 m × 3 m. State the values you use.
items.answer: about 70 kg (using ρ ≈ 1.2 kg m⁻³, V = 60 m³)
items.markingKey: sensible estimates (ρ ≈ 1.2 kg m⁻³, V = 60 m³) [1]; m = ρV applied [1]; answer within an order of magnitude of 70 kg [1] [3]

items.stem: Zara is writing a report on an optical experiment using light of wavelength 589 nm and a wire of diameter 0.25 mm. (a) Express the wavelength in metres in standard form. (b) Calculate the frequency of the light (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). (c) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire in m². (d) State the frequency using a suitable prefix.
items.markingKey: (a) nm = 10⁻⁹: 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m [1] (b) f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.09 × 10¹⁴ Hz [1] [2] (c) A = πd²/4 with d = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.91 × 10⁻⁸ m² [1] [2] (d) THz = 10¹² Hz: 509 THz [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A quantity is calculated from y = a − b. How is the uncertainty in y found? (b) State what is meant by the precision of a measurement.
items.answer: (a) The absolute uncertainties of a and b are added (b) How close repeated readings are to each other (small spread / scatter).
items.markingKey: (a) For sums and differences, add absolute uncertainties. (b) closeness of repeated readings to each other [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the difference between a systematic error and a random error, giving an example of each. (b) Explain why an ammeter with a zero error can give precise but inaccurate readings.
items.answer: (a) A systematic error shifts all readings the same way (e.g. a zero error on a meter); a random error causes readings to scatter unpredictably about the mean (e.g. reaction time when using a stopwatch). (b) The readings may be close together (small random scatter, so precise), but each is shifted from the true value by the zero error (so not accurate).
items.markingKey: (a) systematic: same direction/size with example [1]; random: scatter with example [1] [2] (b) precise: small scatter [1]; inaccurate: shifted by zero error [1] [2]

items.stem: Four measurements of the mass of a standard sample are 350, 350, 391, 360 (same unit). The accepted value is 340. Describe the readings in terms of accuracy and precision, and suggest what type of error is most likely present.
items.answer: They are not precise and not accurate. A systematic error (e.g. zero or calibration error) is likely because the mean is shifted from the true value. The large scatter shows significant random error.
items.markingKey: precision judged from spread [1]; accuracy judged from mean vs accepted value [1]; correct error type [1] [3]

items.stem: A metal cylinder has mass 24.6 ± 0.1 g, diameter 1.80 ± 0.01 cm and length 5.10 ± 0.05 cm. Its density is ρ = 4m/(πd²L). Calculate the percentage uncertainty in ρ.
items.markingKey: %ρ = %m + 2%d + %L = 0.41 + 2 × 0.56 + 0.98 = 2.5%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The acceleration of free fall is found from g = 4π²l/T². A student measures l = 0.500 ± 0.002 m and the time for 20 oscillations as 28.4 ± 0.4 s. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in g.
items.markingKey: %g = %l + 2 × %t = 0.40% + 2 × 1.4% = 3.2%. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Priya determines the resistivity of a metal wire using ρ = RA/L. The measurements are L = 1.000 ± 0.002 m, diameter d = 0.32 ± 0.01 mm and R = 6.8 ± 0.1 Ω. (a) Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire. (b) Calculate the resistivity.
items.markingKey: (a) A = πd²/4 = π × (3.2 × 10⁻⁴)²/4 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m² [1] [2] (b) ρ = RA/L = 6.8 × 8.04 × 10⁻⁸/1.000 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.47 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a car going around a bend at constant speed has a changing velocity. (b) Describe how to find the resultant of two non-perpendicular forces by scale drawing.
items.answer: (a) Velocity is a vector; its direction changes on the bend so the velocity changes although its magnitude (speed) is constant. (b) Choose a scale, draw the first force to scale, draw the second from its tip at the correct angle (tip to tail), then measure the length and angle of the line from start to end.
items.markingKey: (a) velocity has direction [1]; direction changes [1] [2] (b) scale and tip-to-tail [1]; closing side measured for magnitude [1]; direction measured [1] [3]

items.answer: (a) Choose a scale, draw the first force to scale, draw the second from its tip at the correct angle (tip to tail), then measure the length and angle of the line from start to end. (b) Velocity is a vector; its direction changes on the bend so the velocity changes although its magnitude (speed) is constant.
items.markingKey: (a) scale and tip-to-tail [1]; closing side measured for magnitude [1]; direction measured [1] [3] (b) velocity has direction [1]; direction changes [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah walks 15 km due east and then 16 km due north. Work out the magnitude of the displacement.
items.markingKey: √(15² + 16²) = 21.9 km. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A skier of weight 300 N stands on a slope inclined at 35° to the horizontal. (a) Calculate the component of the weight parallel to the slope. (b) The angle of the slope is increased. Explain how the two components change.
items.answer: (a) 172 N (b) The parallel component (W sin θ) increases and the perpendicular component (W cos θ) decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) W sin θ = 300 sin 35° (method/substitution) [1]; answer 172 N with unit [1] [2] (b) parallel increases [1]; perpendicular decreases [1] [2]
